appSubtitle: Peek inside the Earth with seismic waves

welcome.title: What's inside the Earth?
welcome.lead: Nobody can dig to the center of the Earth. But seismic waves let us look inside it! Become a seismologist and uncover the planet's secrets.
welcome.step1Body: Click or drag on the cross-section to move the focus. Click inside the Earth for a deep earthquake.
welcome.step2Body: Hit "Make a quake!" and watch P-waves (blue) and S-waves (red) travel through the planet.
welcome.step3Body: Double-click the surface to place stations. Where do waves arrive — and where don't they?
welcome.missionTeaser: Clear {{count}} missions and rise to "Geophysics Doctor"!

description.crust: The outermost layer of Earth. Continental crust is 30–70 km thick; oceanic crust is 5–10 km. P-wave: 6.0 km/s, S-wave: 3.5 km/s.
description.upperMantle: Extends from the crust to ~400 km depth. Includes the lithosphere and asthenosphere. P-wave: 8.0 km/s, S-wave: 4.5 km/s.
description.lowerMantle: From 400 to 2900 km depth. Solid rock under high pressure. P-wave: 13.0 km/s, S-wave: 7.0 km/s.
description.outerCore: From 2900 to 5150 km depth. Liquid iron-nickel alloy. S-waves cannot travel through liquids, creating the S-wave shadow zone. P-wave: 9.0 km/s.
description.innerCore: From 5150 km to Earth's center. Solid iron-nickel alloy. P-wave: 11.0 km/s, S-wave: 3.5 km/s.

learning.title: Learning Panel
learning.triviaBody: In 1936 Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann discovered the solid inner core from faint waves arriving inside the P-wave shadow zone.

explanation.intro: Hi there! Start by pressing "Make a quake!". You'll see P-waves (blue) and S-waves (red) travel through the Earth.
explanation.shadowZoneS: No S-waves reach stations beyond 103°. S-waves (shear waves) cannot travel through liquid, so they are absorbed by the liquid outer core. The S-wave shadow zone is evidence that Earth's outer core is liquid.
explanation.shadowZoneP: Between 103° and 143° lies the P-wave shadow zone. The large velocity change at the core-mantle boundary bends P-waves away from this region. PKP waves (P-waves through the core) emerge beyond 143°.
explanation.pkpArrival: PKP wave detected! This P-wave traveled through the outer core and emerged on the far side of Earth, beyond the shadow zone.
explanation.observerInShadow: This station ({{distance}}°) is in the S-wave shadow zone. S-waves can't cross the liquid outer core, so they never arrive.
explanation.bothWaves: This station ({{distance}}°) received both P-waves and S-waves. P arrives first, then S — the gap between them is the S−P time.
explanation.pFirst: P-waves (Primary waves) travel faster than S-waves and arrive first at every distance. S-waves (Secondary waves) travel only through solid material.

quiz.title: Quiz
quiz.intro: Test what you learned in the simulator. {{total}} questions.
quiz.resultGood: Great job! Almost a perfect score!
quiz.resultTry: Experiment in the simulator, then try again!

q1.text: Which seismic waves reach a station at an epicentral distance of 150°?
q1.explanation: Beyond 103°, S-waves cannot arrive (absorbed by the liquid outer core). Direct P-waves are shadowed between 103° and 143°, but PKP waves refracted through the core emerge beyond 143°. At 150°, only PKP is recorded.

q2.text: Why does the S-wave shadow zone exist?
q2.explanation: S-waves are shear (transverse) waves that cannot travel through liquids. The outer core is composed of liquid iron-nickel alloy, so S-waves are absorbed there. This creates the S-wave shadow zone beyond ~103°.

q3.text: At an epicentral distance of 80°, which wave arrives first?
q3.explanation: P-waves always travel faster than S-waves (e.g., P: 6.0 km/s vs S: 3.5 km/s in the crust). P-waves always arrive first — hence the names Primary (P) and Secondary (S) waves.

q4.text: What is the main reason seismic waves curve (refract) as they travel through Earth?
q4.explanation: By Snell's Law, waves refract at boundaries where velocity changes. Inside Earth, increasing pressure and temperature change wave velocities continuously with depth, causing seismic rays to curve rather than travel in straight lines.

q5.text: Which correctly describes the states of the outer and inner core?
q5.explanation: The outer core is liquid (S-waves can't pass), while the inner core is solid. Despite its high temperature, the enormous pressure keeps the inner core solid.

q6.text: How does the S−P time (gap between P and S arrivals) change farther from the focus?
q6.explanation: P and S travel at different speeds, so the gap grows with distance. Measuring the S−P time on a seismograph tells you how far away the quake was (Omori's formula). Check it in the Seismograph tab!

q7.text: Roughly what range of epicentral distances is the P-wave shadow zone? (teaching model)
q7.explanation: P-waves refract sharply at the core-mantle boundary, so they don't reach 103°–143° directly. Gutenberg used this shadow to estimate the size of the core.

q8.text: In this simulator's Earth model, in which layer do P-waves travel fastest?
q8.explanation: In this model the lower mantle has the highest P-wave speed (13.0 km/s). Entering the liquid outer core, P slows sharply to 9.0 km/s — and that drop creates the P-wave shadow zone.
